chapters.title: Chapter 2: A Wider Lens on Risk

lessons.title: Correlation and Diversification: When Alternatives Help and When They Fall Together

children.text: Nikhil, a 34-year-old founder in Bengaluru, is proud of his "diversified" portfolio: a Nifty 50 index fund, a mid-cap fund, a PE fund, pre-IPO shares in two startups, and a small angel cheque into a friend's SaaS company. Six holdings, five different wrappers. Then 2022 arrives: global tech stocks sell off, interest rates rise, and India's startup funding dries up. His listed funds wobble, his PE fund's reported value slips, his pre-IPO shares get no bids, and his friend's startup cannot raise its next round. Nikhil did not own six different bets. He owned one bet, Indian company earnings and valuations, dressed up six ways.

body.text: Diversification comes from owning assets driven by different things, not assets with different names. And correlations measured in calm years have a habit of jumping just when you need diversification most.

children.text: What Correlation Measures

markDefs.definition: A number between −1 and +1 that measures how consistently two assets' returns move together. +1 means perfectly together, 0 means no consistent relationship, −1 means perfectly opposite.

children.text: The
correlation coefficient
, usually written ρ (rho), tells you whether two assets tend to rise and fall at the same time. It says nothing about how much each one moves, only whether they move together.

cells: Tend to move in opposite directions
Very strong, but rare and often unstable

children.text: How Correlation Cuts Portfolio Risk
For a portfolio of two assets, total volatility depends on each asset's weight (w), its volatility (σ) and the correlation between them (ρ):

body.caption: Two-asset portfolio volatility. Only the last term depends on correlation.

children.text: Put 70% in a Nifty 50 fund with 18% volatility and 30% in a second asset with 15% volatility. Keep every number the same and change only the correlation.

body.title: Volatility of a 70:30 portfolio as correlation changes (%)

children.text: At a correlation of +1, the portfolio is exactly as volatile as the weighted average of its parts, 17.1%. There is no diversification at all. At zero correlation, it drops to 13.4%, with no change in either asset. That fall in risk is the only free lunch in investing, and it comes entirely from correlation. An alternative with a high correlation to the Nifty adds complexity and fees without buying you much of it.

body.title: Calculate the diversification benefit
body.prompt: A portfolio holds 50% in Asset A and 50% in Asset B. Each has 20% volatility, and their correlation is 0. What is the portfolio's volatility, in percent? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: √(0.5² × 20² + 0.5² × 20² + 0) = √(100 + 100) = √200 ≈ 14.1%. Two assets that are each 20% volatile combine into a portfolio about 30% less volatile, purely because they do not move together.

children.text: How Correlated Are Alternatives With Indian Equities, Really?

Pitch decks love to show alternatives with near-zero correlation to the stock market. Lesson 3 explained why: appraised values lag, so they rarely fall in the same quarter as the Nifty. Once you think about what actually drives each asset, the picture changes.

body.caption: Correlation with the Nifty 50: what reports suggest vs what the underlying drivers imply (illustrative ranges)

cells: Around zero, sometimes negative in crises
Global fear, US dollar, rupee, central bank buying
Low, but can rise when inflation is the problem
Rents, interest rates and market sentiment
Moderate, rising sharply in credit crises
Borrower health and the credit cycle
Company earnings and valuations, like listed equity
High, especially with small caps and global tech
Low to moderate over long periods
Local demand, incomes and home loan rates

body.text: A quick test: ask what makes the asset's cash flows go up or down. If the answer is "Indian companies growing and investors paying more for that growth," it is equity risk, whatever the wrapper. PE, VC, pre-IPO shares and angel stakes are mostly equity risk with a lock-in attached.

children.text: Four Reasons "Diversifiers" Fall Together
Same underlying driver.
Private companies live in the same economy as listed ones. When valuations fall on NSE, they fall in the next private funding round too, just later.
Liquidity panics.
In a panic, investors sell whatever they can sell, not what they want to sell. For a few weeks in March 2020, even gold fell alongside equities before recovering strongly.
A shared hidden factor.

Rising interest rates hurt long bonds, REITs, leveraged property and high-valuation startups at the same time. A credit crunch hits NBFC shares, real estate developers and private credit funds together.
Smoothing hides it.
An appraised asset that falls a quarter or two after the Nifty shows a low reported correlation, even when both were hit by the same shock.

body.label: RBI repo rate increase, May 2022 to February 2023
body.context: A 2.5 percentage point rise in under a year. Assets that looked unrelated, from long-duration debt funds to REITs and late-stage startups, all felt the same pressure from higher rates.

children.text: The Crisis Test: How Indian Assets Behaved

body.caption: How major asset types broadly behaved in recent Indian stress episodes (simplified)

Fell about 38% by March, recovered by year-end

children.text: The pattern is consistent. Gold was the one holding that genuinely behaved differently in most episodes, although not in the first weeks of the 2020 panic. Credit, real estate and private markets tended to suffer alongside equities or right after them, often with a lag that made them look safer at the time.

columns.label: Genuinely different drivers
points: Gold: driven by fear, currency and central banks
High-quality government bonds: driven by rates and inflation
Long leases to strong tenants: contracted rent, not growth bets
Infrastructure with regulated or inflation-linked cash flows, such as some InvIT assets

columns.label: Mostly equity risk in another wrapper
points: VC funds, angel stakes and pre-IPO shares
Real estate development projects that depend on buyer sentiment
Lower-rated private credit to companies that struggle when the economy slows

body.title: Find the real diversifier
body.question: An investor holds 80% of their portfolio in Indian listed equity funds. Which addition is most likely to genuinely reduce portfolio risk in a stock market crash?
options: A growth-stage PE fund investing in Indian consumer companies
Pre-IPO shares of a fintech startup
A small-cap focused Category III AIF
body.explanation: The PE fund, pre-IPO shares and small-cap AIF are all driven by Indian company earnings and valuations, the same thing that drives the investor's existing equity funds. Gold's returns depend on different forces, and it has historically had near-zero correlation with Indian equities.

body.title: Read the correlation
body.textWithBlank: Two assets with a correlation of ___ move in perfect lockstep and offer no diversification benefit at all.
body.explanation: At a correlation of +1, portfolio volatility equals the weighted average of the two assets' volatilities. Any correlation below +1 reduces risk, and the lower it goes, the bigger the benefit.

body.title: Rebuild Nikhil's portfolio
body.scenario: Recall Nikhil from the start of this lesson. His ₹2 crore portfolio is split: ₹60 lakh Nifty 50 index fund, ₹40 lakh mid-cap fund, ₹50 lakh PE fund commitment, ₹30 lakh pre-IPO shares in two startups, and ₹20 lakh in an angel investment. He has no debt and no gold, and his own salary and ESOPs depend on the startup ecosystem.
body.prompt: Explain why his portfolio is less diversified than it looks, and suggest what kind of changes would genuinely diversify it.
body.modelAnswer:
Why it is concentrated:
1. Every holding is Indian equity risk. The index fund and mid-cap fund are listed equity. The PE fund, pre-IPO shares and angel stake are private equity, driven by the same earnings, valuations and funding conditions.
2. The ₹1 crore in PE, pre-IPO and angel (50% of the portfolio) is also illiquid and heavily tilted to startups and growth companies.
3. His human capital is correlated too. His salary and ESOPs rise and fall with the same startup ecosystem, so a funding winter could hit his job and half his portfolio at once.
4. Reported correlations will look low because the private holdings are appraised, which hides the concentration.

What would genuinely diversify:
- Add assets with different drivers: high-quality government or AAA debt funds, and a gold ETF.
- Avoid adding new private market commitments until the startup-heavy share is lower. Let existing commitments run off.
- Keep an emergency fund in liquid assets, since his income itself is at risk in the same scenario.
- Within equity, a broad index is a better core than more single-company bets.

points: Correlation measures whether two assets move together, from −1 to +1. Lower correlation means more diversification benefit.
In a 70:30 portfolio, dropping correlation from +1 to 0 cut volatility from 17.1% to 13.4% without changing either asset.
Many alternatives report low correlation only because appraisals lag listed markets.
PE, VC, pre-IPO shares and angel stakes are mostly equity risk with a lock-in attached.
Liquidity panics, shared factors like interest rates, and credit crunches can make supposed diversifiers fall together.
Judge diversification by what drives each asset's cash flows, and remember your job and income belong in that picture too.
